question: Which body system undergoes the biggest and fastest change right when a baby is born?

options.A: Renal filtration system
options.B: Cardiopulmonary system
options.C: Gastrointestinal tract
options.D: Musculoskeletal framework

explanation: The heart and lungs must instantly adapt to oxygenate the body independently of the placenta right at birth. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why is keeping a newborn warm right after delivery so important?

options.A: Cold skin stops the umbilical cord from pulsing naturally
options.B: Cold stress burns energy stores and causes metabolic acidosis
options.C: Low body temperature triggers immediate meconium passage
options.D: Chilling prevents the baby from opening its eyes

explanation: A cold baby uses up brown fat and glucose rapidly to stay warm, which quickly leads to dangerous acid buildup in the blood. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h1)

question: How many quick evaluation questions does a midwife ask immediately when a baby is born?

options.A: Four
options.B: Two
options.C: Five
options.D: Three

explanation: The initial assessment checks gestation, breathing or crying effort, and muscle tone. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h2)

question: A baby is born limp and not breathing after a long labor. What should the midwife do first?

options.A: Place the baby skin-to-skin on the mother's chest
options.B: Weigh the infant and administer vitamin K injection
options.C: Take the baby to the warmer for immediate resuscitation
options.D: Instill eye ointment and wrap the baby tightly in blankets

explanation: Poor tone and absent breathing mean the baby needs immediate advanced care away from the mother. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the highest possible total score on the APGAR scale?

options.A: Twelve
options.B: Hundred
options.C: Ten
options.D: Five

explanation: There are five criteria, and each can score a maximum of two points, totaling ten. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h3)

question: What is the main reason for calculating an APGAR score?

options.A: To calculate the exact gestational age of the infant
options.B: To guide immediate decisions about newborn resuscitation
options.C: To diagnose specific genetic disorders in the delivery room
options.D: To predict the child's academic performance in school

explanation: The score helps the healthcare team quickly see if the baby needs help transitioning or breathing. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h3)

question: What heart rate gives a baby a score of 2 for the Pulse part of the APGAR test?

options.A: Above 100 beats per minute
options.B: Zero beats per minute
options.C: Between 60 and 80 beats per minute
options.D: Exactly 50 beats per minute

explanation: A healthy newborn heart rate is fast, scoring a full 2 points when it goes over 100 beats per minute. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h4)

question: A newborn has a pink body with bluish hands and feet, a heart rate of 110, grimaces when suctioned, keeps legs flexed, and breathes with a strong cry. What is the Appearance score?
explanation: A pink body with blue extremities represents acrocyanosis, which is given a score of 1. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h4)

question: At what specific times are routine APGAR scores checked on a newborn?

options.A: One and five minutes after birth
options.B: Immediately and thirty minutes later
options.C: Ten and twenty minutes after birth
options.D: Two and ten minutes after delivery

explanation: Standard protocol mandates scoring at 1 minute to check tolerance and 5 minutes to check ongoing adaptation. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h5)

question: A baby gets a total APGAR score of 4 at the five-minute mark. What should the midwife do next regarding scoring?

options.A: Wait an hour before checking the baby's score again
options.B: Continue assessing and scoring every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes
options.C: Discharge the mother and baby home immediately
options.D: Stop scoring completely because the 5-minute mark is final

explanation: When scores remain depressed below 7 at five minutes, protocols require continued scoring every 5 minutes until 20 minutes pass. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which APGAR score range shows moderate depression that needs active help?

options.A: 7 to 10
options.B: 0 to 3
options.C: 4 to 6
options.D: 8 to 10

explanation: A score between 4 and 6 signals moderate compromise, requiring oxygen support and stimulation. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h6)

question: What does an APGAR score of 2 at one minute tell the midwife?

options.A: The baby has mild distress and only requires warm blankets
options.B: The infant is severely depressed and needs immediate resuscitation
options.C: The newborn is transitioning normally and needs routine skin-to-skin
options.D: The delivery was completely free of any complications

explanation: A score of 0 to 3 falls in the severe depression range, necessitating immediate life-saving resuscitation. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T1#BMP214_U1_T1_h6)

question: When should you do the full physical check on a newborn?

options.A: Prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord
options.B: Within the first twenty-four hours of life
options.C: Only when the mother is discharged home
options.D: Exactly at one hour after delivery

explanation: Doing a thorough check within the first day helps catch any hidden health concerns early. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is keeping the room warm so important during a newborn check?

options.A: To keep the midwife comfortable while working in the labor room
options.B: To make the baby sleep soundly through the entire procedure
options.C: To prevent the baby from developing dangerous hypothermia
options.D: To dry up any remaining vernix caseosa on the skin much faster

explanation: Newborns lose body heat very quickly. Keeping them warm protects them from getting dangerously cold. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h1)

question: What is the normal resting position for a healthy term newborn?

options.A: Fully extended arms and legs resting flat
options.B: Rigid extension of both legs and both arms
options.C: Limp posture with zero resistance to movement
options.D: Flexed posture with limbs tightly drawn in

explanation: Term babies naturally keep their arms and legs curled in because of normal muscle tone from the womb. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h2)

question: You check a newborn boy and notice his testes are down in a folded scrotum. What does this mean?

options.A: It is an abnormal swelling caused by birth trauma.
options.B: It suggests the baby was actually born prematurely.
options.C: It is a normal, expected finding for a term male newborn.
options.D: It indicates an endocrine disorder requiring immediate surgery.

explanation: Descended testes and a wrinkled scrotum are signs of a full-term baby boy. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h2)

question: What are the tiny white spots often seen on a newborn's nose and chin called?

options.A: Vernix
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Lanugo
options.D: Milia

explanation: Milia are small, harmless blocked oil glands that go away on their own without any treatment. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which of these skin findings is a normal variant in African newborns and not a cause for alarm?

options.A: Mongolian spots over the lower back
options.B: Severe petechiae scattered over the face
options.C: Persistent central cyanosis of the lips
options.D: Generalized yellow staining of the sclera

explanation: Mongolian spots are harmless birthmarks that are very common on pigmented skin and fade over time. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the normal head circumference range for a healthy term newborn?

options.A: 50 to 55 centimeters
options.B: 40 to 45 centimeters
options.C: 33 to 35 centimeters
options.D: 20 to 25 centimeters

explanation: A healthy term baby's head usually measures between 33 and 35 centimeters around. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h4)

question: How does a term newborn's chest circumference usually compare to their head circumference?

options.A: It is slightly smaller than the head circumference.
options.B: It is always much larger than the head circumference.
options.C: It is exactly equal to the head circumference.
options.D: It varies unpredictably with no fixed relationship.

explanation: In a healthy term baby, the chest is normally about two centimeters smaller than the head. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h4)

question: What clothing should a newborn have on when being weighed?

options.A: Completely naked without any clothes or diapers
options.B: Wearing a standard cloth nappy for comfort
options.C: Dressed in a light vest and clean dry diaper
options.D: Wrapped tightly in a warm hospital blanket

explanation: All clothes and diapers must be removed to get an accurate birth weight. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h5)

question: A student measures a baby's head by wrapping the tape under the chin and across the forehead. What should you do?

options.A: Document the reading immediately because any head measurement method is valid.
options.B: Praise the student for following the correct clinical procedure for head measurement.
options.C: Suggest that a chest measurement be substituted for the head measurement.
options.D: Correct the student, explaining the tape must pass over the occiput and above the eyebrows.

explanation: Head circumference must be measured across the back of the head and just above the eyebrows for accuracy. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h5)

question: What do we call a newborn whose weight falls below the 10th percentile for their gestational age?

options.A: Macrosomic for gestational age
options.B: Small for gestational age
options.C: Large for gestational age
options.D: Appropriate for gestational age

explanation: Weights below the 10th percentile on growth charts mean the baby is small for gestational age. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why is plotting a newborn's weight on a growth chart important?

options.A: It helps anticipate specific risks like low blood sugar or macrosomia.
options.B: It guarantees that the mother will produce enough breastmilk for feeding.
options.C: It replaces the need to perform a complete physical head-to-toe examination.
options.D: It determines the exact date when the baby will be discharged from the ward.

explanation: Knowing the growth percentile helps midwives watch out for potential blood sugar or growth-related issues. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h6)

question: Where should you officially record a newborn's measurements?

options.A: Only in the nurse's private shift handover diary
options.B: In the baby's case note and child health card
options.C: On a personal notebook kept by the mother at home
options.D: On the delivery room blackboard for public viewing

explanation: Official hospital case notes and child health cards are the proper places to record vital newborn data. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h7)

question: You notice a soft swelling on a newborn's head that crosses the suture lines. What is the best first step?

options.A: Document the finding accurately and report it to the doctor.
options.B: Tell the mother that her baby suffered permanent brain damage.
options.C: Attempt to drain the fluid using a sterile syringe immediately.
options.D: Ignore the swelling because all head bumps disappear within hours.

explanation: Findings like a caput succedaneum should be documented clearly and reported for proper medical follow-up. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T2#BMP214_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary origin of primitive reflexes in a newborn?

options.A: Central nervous system
options.B: Gastrointestinal tract
options.C: Peripheral vascular system
options.D: Skeletal muscle tissue

explanation: Primitive reflexes are automatic movements controlled by the central nervous system, specifically subcortical structures present at birth. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why do newborn primitive reflexes fade as the baby gets older?

options.A: Maturation of the cerebral cortex inhibits them
options.B: Breast milk changes the chemical balance in the brain
options.C: Muscles become too heavy for the reflexes to move
options.D: Daily physical handling stops the automatic triggers

explanation: As the higher brain centers develop and mature, they take control and suppress these automatic newborn reflex patterns. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h1)

question: What physical sensation triggers the Moro reflex in a newborn?

options.A: A sudden feeling of falling or loss of support
options.B: A sharp pinch on the bottom of the foot
options.C: A loud scratching sound near the ear
options.D: A bright flash of light shining in the eyes

explanation: The Moro reflex specifically responds to an abrupt change in equilibrium, mimicking a fall or sudden drop in support. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h2)

question: How should a midwife test the Moro reflex safely?

options.A: Drop the infant several feet onto a soft mattress
options.B: Clap loudly directly against the infant's ear
options.C: Allow a controlled, very slight head drop while supporting the body
options.D: Quickly pull both arms straight out of their sockets

explanation: A safe assessment requires only a minimal, well-supported drop of the head relative to the trunk to elicit the response. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h2)

question: Where should the newborn be positioned when starting the Moro reflex test?

options.A: Hanging upside down by the ankles
options.B: Immersed in a warm bath of water
options.C: On a flat, comfortable examining table
options.D: Standing upright on the floor with shoes

explanation: The examination always begins with the infant safely laid out on a supportive, flat surface. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h3)

question: What should the midwife do right after allowing the infant's head to drop slightly during the test?

options.A: Record the Apgar score in the delivery register
options.B: Administer Vitamin K injection into the thigh
options.C: Catch the head quickly on the hand before it strikes the surface
options.D: Turn the baby face down to check breathing rate

explanation: Safety requires the midwife to cradle the head immediately after the small drop so the infant does not hit the table. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h3)

question: What happens during the first phase of a normal Moro reflex response?

options.A: The infant curls into a tight ball
options.B: Legs kick rapidly like running
options.C: Arms abduct and extend with open fingers
options.D: Arms cross tightly over the abdomen

explanation: The initial reaction to the drop is a sudden outward throwing of the arms with open hands. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h4)

question: What does an asymmetrical Moro response, where one arm moves normally and the other stays limp, most likely suggest?

options.A: An impending respiratory tract infection
options.B: A clavicle fracture or brachial plexus injury
options.C: A high level of maternal vitamin deficiency
options.D: A normal variation found in preterm infants

explanation: When only one side moves, it frequently points to localized trauma like a broken collarbone or nerve damage from birth. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why is an absent Moro reflex in a full-term newborn concerning?

options.A: It proves the baby will have a permanent speech impediment
options.B: It suggests a serious problem within the central or peripheral nervous system
options.C: It indicates the mother received too much pain relief in labor
options.D: It simply means the baby is too hungry to move properly

explanation: A complete lack of response means nerve pathways or brain centers are not functioning as expected. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which condition is most commonly linked with an exaggerated or jittery Moro response?

options.A: Normal physiological weight loss
options.B: Transient newborn skin rashes
options.C: Physiological jaundice of the newborn
options.D: Neonatal abstinence syndrome

explanation: Withdrawal from substances or extreme irritability can make the nervous system overreact, causing jittery and exaggerated reflexes. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h5)

question: What specific detail must be included when charting a Moro reflex assessment?

options.A: The time the placenta was delivered
options.B: Symmetry and quality of the response
options.C: The exact brand of the weighing scale
options.D: The mother's blood group and genotype

explanation: Documentation must focus on how the baby moved, noting whether both sides reacted equally and strongly. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h6)

question: What action should the midwife take immediately after finding a completely absent Moro reflex in a full-term baby?

options.A: Escalate the finding to the paediatric team without delay
options.B: Discharge the mother and baby home with routine advice
options.C: Wait twenty-four hours to see if the reflex appears on its own
options.D: Document that the baby is completely healthy and normal

explanation: An absent reflex is a red flag that requires urgent medical review and investigation. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T3#BMP214_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which primitive oral reflex helps a newborn locate the maternal nipple by turning toward a cheek stroke?

options.A: Sucking reflex
options.B: Rooting reflex
options.C: Gag reflex
options.D: Extrusion reflex

explanation: The rooting reflex makes the baby turn their head toward the side where the cheek or mouth is touched, helping them find the nipple. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the main reason newborns have primitive oral reflexes like sucking and rooting?

options.A: To keep the baby awake
options.B: To test brain function
options.C: To help them feed and survive
options.D: To help develop speech early

explanation: These reflexes work together to help the newborn find food and feed right after birth, which is essential for survival. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h1)

question: What kind of pressure does a baby create in the mouth to draw milk from the breast?

options.A: Atmospheric pressure
options.B: Hydrostatic pressure
options.C: Negative pressure
options.D: Positive pressure

explanation: Dropping the lower jaw creates a vacuum inside the mouth, generating negative pressure that pulls milk out. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h2)

question: Why does a newborn need to coordinate cranial nerves during a feed?

options.A: To control the temperature of the breast milk
options.B: To manage sucking, swallowing, and breathing smoothly
options.C: To release digestive juices in the stomach
options.D: To keep eyes focused on the mother's face

explanation: Feeding requires precise timing between sucking, swallowing, and breathing to prevent choking, managed by multiple cranial nerves. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h2)

question: How should a midwife correctly position her finger when testing a newborn's sucking reflex?

options.A: Touching only the outer edges of the lips
options.B: Pad side up against the hard palate
options.C: Pressing downward on the lower gum line
options.D: Flat across the tip of the tongue

explanation: Placing a clean finger with the pad facing upward against the infant's palate stimulates the natural suck response. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h3)

question: A midwife notices a baby has strong suction, but milk leaks constantly from the corners of the mouth during feeds. What should be checked first?

options.A: Serum blood glucose levels immediately
options.B: Lip seal and positioning at the breast
options.C: The patency of the infant's nasal passages
options.D: Deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs

explanation: If suction is strong but milk leaks, checking the latch or lip seal is the most practical first step. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why might a healthy term newborn show a temporarily weak suck right after birth?

options.A: Permanent damage to the hypoglossal nerve
options.B: Exposure to labor medications or birth fatigue
options.C: Congenital absence of the hard palate
options.D: Severe dehydration from pregnancy

explanation: Labor medications or simple tiredness from a long delivery can temporarily make a newborn sleepy and affect the sucking reflex. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a normal variation in a healthy term infant's sucking?

options.A: A slightly sleepy suck that improves within the first day
options.B: A completely absent suck response lasting several days
options.C: Strong rhythmic bursts alternating with brief pauses
options.D: Good tongue movement and firm pressure on a finger

explanation: A completely absent sucking reflex is abnormal and needs immediate investigation. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h4)

question: A full-term newborn is limp, sleepy, and has no sucking reflex. What is the immediate priority for midwifery care?

options.A: Wait forty-eight hours to see if the reflex develops
options.B: Provide safe alternative feeding and notify the doctor for a review
options.C: Send the mother and baby home to feed on demand
options.D: Apply cold compresses to the cheeks

explanation: A baby unable to suck safely needs alternative nutrition to prevent low blood sugar and an urgent medical check. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why is teaching manual milk expression important when a newborn has a weak sucking reflex?

options.A: To check if the mother has any breast infections
options.B: To maintain milk supply until the baby can feed directly
options.C: To prevent postpartum depression
options.D: To provide extra colostrum for the baby's skin

explanation: Regular milk removal stimulates hormones and keeps milk production going until the baby is strong enough to breastfeed. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T4#BMP214_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which part of the newborn's brain controls basic, automatic movements like primitive reflexes?

options.A: Subcortical regions
options.B: Spinal nerves
options.C: Cerebellar vermis
options.D: Cerebral cortex

explanation: Primitive reflexes are managed by lower, subcortical areas of the brain before the higher cortical areas fully develop. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why do primitive reflexes naturally fade as a baby gets older?

options.A: The baby's muscles become too heavy to move
options.B: The cerebral cortex matures and inhibits them
options.C: Frequent handling desensitizes the skin receptors
options.D: Nutritional deficiencies weaken the reflex arc

explanation: As the brain grows and matures, higher brain functions take over and naturally quiet down these automatic responses. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which cranial nerve carries the touch signals that trigger a baby's rooting reflex?

options.A: Trigeminal nerve
options.B: Facial nerve
options.C: Vagus nerve
options.D: Hypoglossal nerve

explanation: The trigeminal nerve supplies feeling to the face, picking up the touch on the cheek or lip during rooting. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the main survival reason newborns have the rooting reflex?

options.A: Finding food and securing a breastfeeding latch
options.B: Strengthening the muscles of the neck and spine
options.C: Clearing mucus from the upper airway passages
options.D: Protecting the eyes from sudden bright lights

explanation: Turning toward a touch near the mouth helps the newborn find the breast or bottle for feeding easily. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h2)

question: How does a full-term newborn usually react when you gently stroke their upper lip?

options.A: Turns the head sharply toward the opposite shoulder
options.B: Tilts the head backward and opens the mouth
options.C: Extends both arms upward in a startle motion
options.D: Sucks vigorously on the examiner's bare finger

explanation: Stroking the upper lip prompts the baby to tilt back slightly and open the mouth to take in the nipple. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h3)

question: Why might a healthy newborn show a weak rooting reflex right after a big feed?

options.A: The infant is full and lacks motivation to feed
options.B: Excess body fat dampening facial skin sensors
options.C: Digestion temporarily blocks the trigeminal nerve
options.D: The baby is experiencing normal physiological shock

explanation: Babies who have just finished feeding are full, so their hunger drive is temporarily satisfied and they may ignore feeding cues. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h3)

question: Around what age does the rooting reflex normally disappear in a healthy infant?

options.A: 6 to 8 years
options.B: 9 to 12 months
options.C: 3 to 4 months
options.D: 1 to 2 weeks

explanation: As the higher brain centers mature over the first few months of life, the rooting reflex naturally fades away. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h4)

question: What does an equal and active rooting response on both sides of the face tell the midwife?

options.A: The baby is definitely ready to be introduced to solid foods
options.B: The mother had an entirely uncomplicated pregnancy and birth
options.C: The lower motor pathways and brainstem are functioning normally
options.D: The infant has received all necessary routine childhood immunizations

explanation: Equal responses on both sides show that the relevant brainstem structures and nerve pathways are working well. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h4)

question: What might an uneven (asymmetrical) rooting reflex suggest in a newborn delivered with vacuum assistance?

options.A: Local facial nerve injury
options.B: Congenital heart failure
options.C: Severe maternal infection
options.D: Generalized brain tumors

explanation: An uneven reflex on one side of the face often points to mild, temporary nerve trauma from an instrumental delivery. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which of these conditions would most likely cause an absent rooting reflex across both sides of the face?

options.A: Severe birth asphyxia and central nervous depression
options.B: Mild physiologic jaundice fading on the third day
options.C: Normal mild weight loss in the first 48 hours
options.D: Transient skin rashes like erythema toxicum

explanation: When the central nervous system is depressed due to a lack of oxygen, automatic responses like rooting are weakened or temporarily lost. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h5)

question: When is the best time to use the rooting reflex to help start breastfeeding successfully?

options.A: During the golden hour immediately following birth
options.B: When the baby cries continuously for two hours
options.C: Just before the infant is discharged home from the ward
options.D: After the infant has received a full routine bath

explanation: Right after birth, during the golden hour, babies are naturally alert and ready to respond to feeding cues. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h6)

question: A mother shares that her newborn cries frantically and refuses to latch. What advice should you give based on rooting behavior?

options.A: Stop breastfeeding entirely and switch straight to artificial formula
options.B: Wait until the baby is completely exhausted so it will sleep at the breast
options.C: Look for early rooting cues like head turning before the baby starts crying
options.D: Force the baby's mouth open immediately regardless of head movement

explanation: Spotting early feeding cues keeps the baby calm and prevents them from getting overtired, making it much easier to latch. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h6)

question: What primary body systems are evaluated during a newborn neurological check?

options.A: Heart and major blood vessels
options.B: Lungs and upper airways
options.C: Brain and spinal cord
options.D: Stomach and intestines

explanation: The neurological assessment focuses directly on the central nervous system, which includes the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do midwives perform a neurological assessment on a newborn soon after birth?

options.A: To determine the precise blood group of the infant
options.B: To measure the exact birth weight of the baby
options.C: To test the digestive system function of the baby
options.D: To check for early signs of brain injury or developmental delays

explanation: Early neurological checks help identify any birth trauma or congenital nervous system issues right away. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which part of the brain controls primitive reflexes in a newborn?

options.A: Cerebral cortex
options.B: Subcortical regions
options.C: Peripheral nerve endings
options.D: Skull bone structure

explanation: Primitive reflexes are managed by lower, subcortical areas of the brain before the higher cortex fully takes over. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h2)

question: What happens to primitive reflexes as a healthy infant grows older?

options.A: They turn into voluntary skills within one week
options.B: They gradually disappear as higher brain centers mature
options.C: They become much stronger and permanent
options.D: They remain completely unchanged throughout childhood

explanation: As the baby's brain develops, primitive reflexes integrate and fade out, replaced by controlled voluntary movements. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h2)

question: Where should a midwife place a finger to correctly test the palmar grasp reflex?

options.A: Across the back of the baby's hand
options.B: Against the palm of the baby's hand
options.C: Between the fingers of the baby
options.D: Around the wrist of the newborn

explanation: Stimulating the palm triggers the automatic closing of the infant's fingers. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h3)

question: A midwife presses her thumb against the ball of a newborn's foot just below the toes. What physical reaction should she expect to observe?

options.A: The entire leg will kick upward
options.B: The foot will twist outward
options.C: The toes will fan out wide
options.D: The toes will curl downward

explanation: Applying pressure to the ball of the foot elicits the plantar grasp, causing the toes to flex downward. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h3)

question: Around what age does the palmar grasp reflex normally start to fade?

options.A: Three to four months
options.B: Immediately after birth
options.C: Nine to twelve months
options.D: At two years of age

explanation: The palmar grasp typically integrates around 3 to 4 months when voluntary grasping begins. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why does the plantar grasp remain present longer than the palmar grasp?

options.A: The feet grow at a much slower rate than the hands
options.B: It supports stability and motor development for standing and walking
options.C: Babies use their feet to grasp objects just like hands
options.D: Foot nerves connect directly to the heart instead of the brain

explanation: The plantar reflex stays longer to assist with foot stability before the toddler learns to walk. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h4)

question: A newborn baby shows a strong palmar grasp on the right hand but has no response at all on the left hand after a difficult shoulder dystocia delivery. What condition does this finding most likely suggest?

options.A: General brain infection affecting both sides
options.B: Complete absence of the spinal cord
options.C: Normal variation in bilateral reflex strength
options.D: Brachial plexus injury on the left side

explanation: An asymmetric reflex following a difficult birth often points to nerve damage like a brachial plexus palsy on the weak side. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h5)

question: What does a completely absent grasp reflex in both hands and feet usually indicate?

options.A: A temporary lack of milk feeding
options.B: An infant who is simply sleeping too deeply
options.C: Severe nervous system depression or birth asphyxia
options.D: Normal tiredness after a long labor process

explanation: A total lack of primitive reflexes is a major red flag signaling serious central nervous system depression. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T6#BMP214_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of assessing gestational age in a newborn?

options.A: To determine maturity and guide immediate care
options.B: To diagnose congenital infections present at birth
options.C: To measure the length of the umbilical cord
options.D: To calculate the exact birth weight of the infant

explanation: Gestational age assessment helps midwives understand the baby's developmental stage to anticipate and manage prematurity risks. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why might a midwife rely on a physical exam for gestational age in some rural clinics?

options.A: Physical exams are the only legally accepted method in clinics
options.B: Mothers often lack reliable records of their last menstrual period
options.C: Babies change their physical traits rapidly within the first hour
options.D: Ultrasound machines are mandatory for every routine delivery

explanation: When antenatal history is missing or uncertain, newborn physical and neurological exams provide vital clues about gestational age. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h1)

question: What are the two main categories assessed in the New Ballard Score system?

options.A: Neuromuscular and physical maturity
options.B: Cardiovascular and respiratory stability
options.C: Apgar score and metabolic profile
options.D: Anthropometric and genetic markers

explanation: The Ballard score combines assessments of muscle tone and physical body features to estimate gestational age accurately. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h2)

question: When is the best time to perform a neuromuscular assessment on a premature infant using the Ballard scale?

options.A: Only after the baby passes meconium
options.B: Exactly after 72 hours of extrauterine life
options.C: Within the first 12 hours of life
options.D: Prior to initiating any breastfeeding attempts

explanation: Preterm infant muscle tone can alter significantly within the first day, so early assessment yields the most reliable results. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which newborn test involves bending the baby's wrist toward the forearm to measure the angle?

options.A: Scarf sign
options.B: Square window
options.C: Arm recoil
options.D: Popliteal angle

explanation: The square window test evaluates wrist flexibility, with more mature infants showing a smaller angle due to increased muscle tone. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h3)

question: A midwife tests a newborn's arm recoil and notices the arms drop loosely without springing back into flexion. What does this finding suggest?

options.A: The infant is likely of very preterm gestational age
options.B: The mother had gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: The infant has normal term neuromuscular maturity
options.D: The baby experienced birth asphyxia during delivery

explanation: Poor or absent recoil indicates low muscle tone, which is typical of premature babies. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h3)

question: What physical feature on the soles of the feet helps determine gestational maturity in a newborn?

options.A: Plantar creases
options.B: Vernix caseosa
options.C: Dermal melanocytosis
options.D: Lanugo distribution

explanation: Transverse creases spread across the sole of the foot as gestational age increases, starting from the front portion. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h4)

question: How does ear cartilage change as a fetus approaches full term?

options.A: It stays soft, flat, and completely without cartilage
options.B: It shrinks in overall size compared to the head
options.C: It becomes thick and stiff with instant recoil
options.D: It turns completely transparent and fluid-filled

explanation: Cartilage develops late in pregnancy, causing the ear to become firm and spring back fast when bent. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h4)

question: What is the range of possible scores assigned to each individual Ballard criterion?

options.A: -1 to 5
options.B: 1 to 3
options.C: 0 to 10
options.D: 0 to 5

explanation: Each item on the New Ballard Score sheet is graded from -1 for extremely premature traits up to 5. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h5)

question: What must a midwife do after adding up the neuromuscular and physical scores?

options.A: Submit the raw score directly to the national health registry
options.B: Divide the sum by twelve to find the average maturity grade
options.C: Add the baby's birth weight to the total score sum
options.D: Locate the total score on the reference table for gestational age weeks

explanation: The final score matches up with a specific gestational age listed on the reference chart. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h5)

question: How is a newborn delivered at 35 completed weeks of pregnancy classified?

options.A: Post-mature
options.B: Preterm
options.C: Term
options.D: Post-term

explanation: Any infant born before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy is classified as preterm, regardless of birth weight. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h6)

question: A newborn assessed via Ballard score is classified as preterm. Which clinical condition should the midwife actively monitor for in this infant?

options.A: Early eruption of primary teeth
options.B: Hypoglycemia and thermal instability
options.C: Excessive weight gain and hypertension
options.D: Delayed closure of the cranial sutures

explanation: Preterm babies have low fat stores and immature organs, placing them at high risk for low blood sugar and body temperature drops. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T7#BMP214_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the normal core body temperature range for a healthy newborn?
explanation: A normal newborn's core temperature should consistently stay within the narrow range of 36.5°C and 37.5°C to prevent cold or heat stress. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why do healthy term newborns rely on brown adipose tissue instead of shivering when they get cold?

options.A: Shivering requires too much energy from the baby's lungs.
options.B: Their muscular and nervous systems are still too immature for effective shivering.
options.C: Shivering only occurs in adults who have fully developed sweat glands.
options.D: Brown adipose tissue is the only type of fat present in a full-term baby.

explanation: Because newborn muscles and nervous systems are not fully developed, they cannot generate heat through shivering and must use brown fat instead. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which mechanism of heat loss is primarily responsible for cooling a wet newborn immediately after birth?

options.A: Conduction
options.B: Radiation
options.C: Evaporation
options.D: Convection

explanation: When amniotic fluid on the skin turns into vapor, it draws a significant amount of heat away from the newborn's body through evaporation. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h2)

question: Placing a newborn directly onto a cold metal weighing scale without a protective cloth causes heat loss through which method?

options.A: Convection
options.B: Radiation
options.C: Conduction
options.D: Evaporation

explanation: Conduction occurs when body heat is transferred directly to a colder solid object touching the baby's skin. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h2)

question: What metabolic condition frequently develops in a newborn experiencing prolonged cold stress due to depleted energy stores?

options.A: Hyperglycemia
options.B: Hyponatremia
options.C: Hyperkalemia
options.D: Hypoglycemia

explanation: The rapid burning of energy stores to stay warm causes blood sugar levels to drop dangerously low in cold stressed infants. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h3)

question: How does severe cold stress directly lead to metabolic acidosis in a newborn?

options.A: Anaerobic metabolism and the release of fatty acids create excess acid in the blood.
options.B: The baby drinks too much cold amniotic fluid during delivery.
options.C: Kidneys stop producing urine entirely when exposed to low room temperatures.
options.D: Cold air causes the baby's stomach acid to spill into the lungs.

explanation: As the body struggles for oxygen and burns brown fat rapidly, acid builds up in the bloodstream, resulting in metabolic acidosis. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following clinical signs is NOT typically seen in a newborn experiencing cold stress?

options.A: Cool skin to the touch
options.B: Lethargy and poor feeding
options.C: Vigorous shivering
options.D: Tachypnea and grunting

explanation: Newborns lack the neurological maturity to shiver, so shivering is not a sign of cold stress in neonates. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h4)

question: A midwife assesses a term newborn who is lethargic, breathing at 75 breaths per minute, and has cool skin over the abdomen. What is the most appropriate initial concern?

options.A: The infant has an unclosed ductus arteriosus that requires immediate surgery.
options.B: The infant is experiencing a normal post-delivery transition phase that requires no action.
options.C: The infant is likely suffering from cold stress and accompanying respiratory distress.
options.D: The infant is showing classic signs of neonatal hyperthermia.

explanation: Cool skin, fast breathing, and lethargy are classic warning signs that a newborn is cold stressed and struggling. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h4)

question: How long should a midwife ideally postpone a newborn's first bath to ensure temperature stability?

options.A: At least 48 hours
options.B: Until the umbilical cord falls off
options.C: At least 6 to 24 hours
options.D: Exactly 1 hour

explanation: Postponing the first bath for 6 to 24 hours prevents rapid evaporative and conductive heat loss while the baby stabilizes. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why is wearing a cap emphasized as a vital component of the warm chain?

options.A: Hospital protocol requires all babies to wear hats for identification purposes.
options.B: Babies are born with hair that is always wet and increases evaporative cooling.
options.C: The newborn's head is large relative to the body and has a large surface area prone to heat loss.
options.D: Caps prevent the baby from turning its head during breastfeeding.

explanation: A baby's head represents a large percentage of its body surface area, making it a primary site for radiant and convective heat loss. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h5)

question: During a power outage in a primary health center in Nigeria, what is the best method to warm a low-birth-weight infant?

options.A: Initiate continuous Kangaroo Mother Care on the mother's bare chest.
options.B: Place the baby directly under an unpowered fluorescent ceiling light.
options.C: Bathe the baby in warm water to raise the body temperature quickly.
options.D: Wrap the baby tightly in multiple layers of cold plastic bags.

explanation: Kangaroo Mother Care uses the mother's natural body heat to safely warm the baby when electricity and incubators are unavailable. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why is closing delivery room windows during the harmattan season especially important for newborn care?

options.A: It prevents dust from clogging oxygen delivery machines.
options.B: It prevents dry, cold wind currents from causing rapid convective heat loss in the newborn.
options.C: It keeps the room dark so the baby can sleep peacefully.
options.D: It stops mosquitoes from entering the sterile delivery area.

explanation: Harmattan winds bring cold, dry air that increases convective and evaporative heat loss if windows remain open. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T1#BMP214_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the most important thing to focus on when a newborn needs resuscitation?

options.A: Initiating immediate chest compressions
options.B: Administering intravenous fluid boluses
options.C: Checking newborn blood glucose levels
options.D: Establishing effective lung ventilation

explanation: Newborn resuscitation prioritizes getting air into the lungs because breathing problems are the main cause of birth asphyxia. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is preparation before delivery so important for midwives?

options.A: Mothers expect doctors to stand by for every single birth
options.B: Hospital regulations require checking all charts twice
options.C: Standard delivery kits always contain broken equipment
options.D: Emergency interventions must happen without any delays

explanation: Because most compromised babies need help in the very first minutes of life, having equipment ready prevents fatal delays. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h1)

question: How long is the time period known as the Golden Minute after a baby is born?

options.A: Five full minutes
options.B: Exactly sixty seconds
options.C: Half an hour
options.D: Ten brief seconds

explanation: The Golden Minute refers to the crucial first sixty seconds of life when initial assessment and vital resuscitation steps must occur. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which finding during the initial check tells a midwife a baby needs immediate help to breathe?

options.A: Loud crying and pink skin
options.B: A warm and dry body surface
options.C: Active movement of the legs
options.D: Gasping or limp muscle tone

explanation: Poor breathing effort like gasping and poor muscle tone indicate the newborn is failing to transition and requires immediate help. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h2)

question: Where is the narrowest part of the upper airway in a newborn?

options.A: At the cricoid ring
options.B: Inside the nasal passages
options.C: Within the main bronchi
options.D: Across the vocal cords

explanation: The cricoid ring forms the narrowest portion of the neonatal airway, creating a tight anatomical bottleneck. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h3)

question: How does the size of a newborn's tongue affect their airway?

options.A: It produces excess mucus that clogs the windpipe
options.B: It makes inserting a feeding tube impossible
options.C: It can easily fall backward and block the pharynx
options.D: It prevents the baby from opening the mouth wide

explanation: A newborn's large relative tongue size creates a high risk of airway obstruction if the head is not positioned properly. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the correct head position used to open a newborn's airway?

options.A: Neutral or slightly extended sniffing position
options.B: Fully hyperextended neck looking upward
options.C: Turned sharply to the left side
options.D: Flexed position with chin touching the chest

explanation: The sniffing position aligns the airway structures best for airflow without blocking the trachea. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is bending a newborn's neck back too far dangerous during resuscitation?

options.A: It causes immediate cardiac arrest in healthy infants
options.B: It increases the production of thick meconium
options.C: It can stretch and collapse the delicate trachea
options.D: It pushes the large tongue forward into the mouth

explanation: Pushing the head back too far kinks or collapses the soft tracheal walls, worsening airway obstruction. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which area should a midwife suction first when clearing secretions from a newborn?

options.A: The nose before the mouth
options.B: Both nostrils at the exact same time
options.C: Deep down inside the trachea
options.D: The mouth before the nose

explanation: Suctioning the mouth first prevents the baby from aspirating pooled mucus if they suddenly gasp when the nose is touched. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h5)

question: What can happen if a suction tube is pushed too far into a newborn's throat?

options.A: Immediate rupture of the lung tissue
options.B: Severe slowing of the heart rate
options.C: Sudden swelling of the vocal cords
options.D: Permanent loss of the gag reflex

explanation: Deep pharyngeal suctioning triggers the vagal nerve, which rapidly drops the newborn heart rate into dangerous bradycardia. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the most important sign that a newborn resuscitation is working?

options.A: Urine output
options.B: Heart rate
options.C: Body temperature
options.D: Skin color

explanation: Heart rate response tells the midwife immediately whether ventilation is successfully oxygenating the newborn. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h6)

question: When should a midwife start positive pressure ventilation for a newborn?

options.A: Whenever the infant is born before thirty-seven weeks
options.B: Only when the baby's skin turns completely blue
options.C: If the heart rate is below 100 beats per minute
options.D: After chest compressions have failed for two minutes

explanation: A heart rate under 100 beats per minute or persistent gasping/apnea indicates that PPV is required right away. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h6)

question: What device helps confirm that a breathing tube is placed correctly in the trachea?

options.A: A routine blood pressure cuff
options.B: A standard mercury thermometer
options.C: A carbon dioxide detector
options.D: A soft infant suction bulb

explanation: Exhaled carbon dioxide detectors confirm that the tube is correctly placed in the trachea rather than the esophagus. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h7)

question: When is a laryngeal mask airway most helpful during a difficult resuscitation?

options.A: As the very first step before trying to dry and stimulate
options.B: Before clearing the mouth and nose of thick meconium
options.C: To replace routine skin-to-skin contact for a healthy baby
options.D: When bag-mask ventilation fails and intubation is unsuccessful

explanation: Laryngeal mask airways act as reliable rescue devices when standard bag-mask and tube placement attempts prove unsuccessful. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h7)

question: What is a major risk for a newborn who needed extensive resuscitation at birth?

options.A: Experiencing rapid weight gain in the first hours
options.B: Sleeping through normal feeding cues for a full week
options.C: Becoming permanently immune to common bacterial infections
options.D: Developing delayed respiratory distress or brain injury

explanation: Resuscitated babies remain vulnerable to complications like oxygen deprivation injuries and lung problems, requiring close monitoring. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h8)

question: Why is keeping accurate notes during a resuscitation event so important?

options.A: It replaces the need to monitor the baby's temperature
options.B: Hospital insurance companies require long essays on every birth
options.C: It provides a clear timeline of the infant's response to care
options.D: Mothers request copies to include in birth celebration albums

explanation: Detailed records of interventions and vital sign responses guide ongoing clinical decisions by the pediatric team. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T2#BMP214_U2_T2_h8)

question: How many blood vessels are normally found inside a healthy newborn umbilical cord?

options.A: Three blood vessels
options.B: Four blood vessels
options.C: One blood vessel
options.D: Two blood vessels

explanation: A normal umbilical cord always contains two arteries and one vein to transport blood between the foetus and the placenta. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the primary function of Wharton's jelly inside the umbilical cord?

options.A: To provide extra oxygen storage for the newborn during birth
options.B: To produce white blood cells that fight early infections
options.C: To speed up the drying process of the cord stump after birth
options.D: To prevent the cord vessels from kinking or compressing

explanation: Wharton's jelly is a thick, protective substance that cushions the blood vessels inside the cord so blood flow is not blocked during pregnancy and labour. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the primary goal of standard umbilical cord care protocols in the newborn period?

options.A: To wrap the cord tightly with bandages to stop bleeding
options.B: To pull the cord gently each day to speed up separation
options.C: To apply strong chemical disinfectants twice daily
options.D: To keep the cord clean and dry until it falls off naturally

explanation: Standard care relies on cleanliness and air drying to prevent bacteria from growing while the tissue mummifies and separates on its own. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h2)

question: A mother asks if she should apply herbal powder to her baby's wet cord stump. How should the midwife respond?

options.A: Suggest mixing the powder with palm oil for better results
options.B: Agree only if the baby develops a mild fever first
options.C: Advise against it because herbs and powders can introduce germs and cause infection
options.D: Encourage it if the powder was prepared by an older family member

explanation: Unsterile home substances like herbs and powders easily carry tetanus spores and other bacteria directly into the open umbilical wound. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which topical antiseptic is recommended by health authorities for umbilical cord care in high-risk community settings in Nigeria?

options.A: Hydrogen peroxide solution
options.B: Pure methylated spirit
options.C: Iodine tincture solution
options.D: 4% chlorhexidine gel

explanation: Chlorhexidine gel is proven to lower the risk of severe bacterial infections and newborn death in communities with high rates of home deliveries. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why might the recommendation for cord care differ between a well-equipped hospital and a rural community in Nigeria?

options.A: Hospital babies have thicker umbilical cords than babies born at home
options.B: Chlorhexidine gel only works on babies delivered by traditional birth attendants
options.C: Dry cord care is completely illegal in all primary healthcare centres
options.D: The risk of harmful bacteria exposure and newborn infection is higher in community settings

explanation: Where hygiene conditions during and after birth are less controlled, antiseptic applications like chlorhexidine provide vital protection against dangerous infections. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the medical term for a bacterial infection of the umbilical stump and surrounding abdominal tissues?

options.A: Cellulitis
options.B: Mastitis
options.C: Omphalitis
options.D: Conjunctivitis

explanation: Omphalitis specifically refers to infection of the umbilicus and surrounding tissues in newborns, requiring urgent medical intervention. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which finding should alert a midwife to suspect an early umbilical cord infection in a five-day-old newborn?

options.A: Slight bleeding when the diaper rubs against the drying cord
options.B: Redness of the skin spreading outward from the base of the cord
options.C: A dry, dark brown cord stump that feels stiff to the touch
options.D: Natural separation of the umbilical stump on the tenth day of life

explanation: Spreading redness (erythema) onto the abdominal skin is a key sign that bacteria have invaded the tissue beyond a normal healing process. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is a key infection prevention measure when cutting the umbilical cord during delivery?

options.A: Waiting at least one hour before cutting the cord
options.B: Washing the cord with strong bleach before clamping
options.C: Applying warm palm oil immediately before cutting
options.D: Using a sterile or properly disinfected cutting instrument

explanation: Unsterile blades or scissors are a major route for transmitting tetanus bacteria and other pathogens directly into the newborn's bloodstream. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h5)

question: Why is immersing a newborn in unbathed basin water discouraged before the umbilical cord falls off?

options.A: Contaminated water can enter the open umbilical wound and introduce bacteria
options.B: Water makes the baby catch a cold more easily during the first week
options.C: Soaking dissolves the cord clamp before the vessels have closed
options.D: Wet skin prevents the mother from seeing the diaper area clearly

explanation: Sponge baths are recommended until the cord separates because immersing the unhealed navel in water increases the risk of bacterial contamination. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the most effective way for a midwife to teach a new mother how to care for her baby's cord at home?

options.A: Provide a practical demonstration and allow the mother to practice under guidance
options.B: Tell her to watch online videos on her mobile phone without discussion
options.C: Give her a printed textbook to read through before leaving the hospital
options.D: Ask a senior family member to explain the local customs instead

explanation: Hands-on demonstration and guided practice ensure the mother truly understands the correct steps and builds confidence in caring for her newborn. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h6)

question: A mother notices her baby is crying when her diaper touches the navel and the area looks slightly red. What advice should the midwife give?

options.A: Rub native chalk on the spot to cool down the inflammation
options.B: Apply hot water compresses and wait another week to see if it improves
options.C: Bring the baby to the clinic immediately for assessment and possible treatment
options.D: Stop feeding breast milk until the redness disappears completely

explanation: Redness and pain around the cord are warning signs of infection that require professional medical evaluation without delay. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T3#BMP214_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the main reason midwives give eye care to a newborn right after birth?

options.A: To test if the baby has normal eye movement
options.B: To improve how clearly the baby can see at birth
options.C: To stop the eyelids from sticking together from sleep
options.D: To prevent severe eye infections from birth canal bacteria

explanation: Eye prophylaxis protects the newborn's eyes from harmful germs picked up during delivery. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why are newborn babies especially prone to eye infections right after delivery?

options.A: Bright delivery room lights damage the natural surface of the eye
options.B: They lack antibodies to fight off normal air germs
options.C: Their tear ducts are completely blocked for the first week of life
options.D: They pass through a birth canal that may contain maternal infections

explanation: Contact with bacteria in the birth tract can expose the baby's unprotected eyes to infection. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which type of newborn eye issue usually happens shortly after eye drops are given and clears up on its own?

options.A: Chemical conjunctivitis
options.B: Gonococcal conjunctivitis
options.C: Chlamydial conjunctivitis
options.D: Herpetic conjunctivitis

explanation: Chemical irritation from eye drops often appears quickly and goes away without special treatment in a couple of days. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h2)

question: A five-day-old baby at the clinic has thick pus coming from both eyes and very swollen eyelids. Which germ is likely the cause?

options.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.B: Normal skin flora
options.C: Staphylococcus albus
options.D: Candida albicans

explanation: Gonococcal eye infections usually show up fast around days 2 to 5 with heavy discharge. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h2)

question: In which direction should a midwife wipe a newborn's eyes during routine cleaning?

options.A: From the inner corner outward toward the ear
options.B: In a circular motion across both closed eyes
options.C: From the eyebrow down across the cheek
options.D: From the outer corner inward toward the nose

explanation: Wiping outward stops dirty fluid from running across the bridge of the nose into the other eye. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why is it important to use a separate clean swab for each eye when cleaning a newborn?

options.A: To stop spreading infection from one eye to the other
options.B: One swab is never enough to remove all the vernix
options.C: Hospital policy requires using two different packets
options.D: To make the cleaning process go much faster

explanation: Using a fresh swab for every eye ensures germs from one side are not transferred to the healthy side. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the most common medication used for newborn eye care in primary health facilities today?

options.A: Tetracycline 1% eye ointment
options.B: Hydrocortisone eye cream
options.C: Normal saline solution
options.D: Atropine 1% eye drops

explanation: Tetracycline ointment is commonly used because it is stable, effective, and causes minimal irritation. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why has silver nitrate solution mostly been replaced by antibiotic ointments in modern newborn care?

options.A: It changes the permanent color of the baby's iris
options.B: It is far too expensive to buy in large quantities
options.C: It kills all the good bacteria inside the baby's stomach
options.D: It frequently causes painful chemical irritation and redness

explanation: Silver nitrate is a strong chemical that often leads to significant inflammation known as chemical conjunctivitis. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h4)

question: Where should eye ointment or drops be placed inside a newborn's eye?

options.A: In the lower conjunctival pocket
options.B: In the inner corner near the tear duct
options.C: On the outer surface of closed eyelids
options.D: Directly onto the center of the cornea

explanation: Pulling down the lower lid creates a small pocket that holds the medication in place for proper absorption. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is an important safety rule when holding a medication tube near a newborn's eye?

options.A: Always warm the metal tip in warm water first
options.B: Press the tip firmly against the lower eyelid
options.C: Hold the tube vertically two inches above the eyebrow
options.D: Never let the tip touch the baby's eyelashes or skin

explanation: Avoiding contact with eye structures prevents contaminating the medication tube with bacteria from the skin. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is a normal, expected reaction right after applying eye prophylaxis ointment to a newborn?

options.A: Complete closure of the eyelids for 24 hours
options.B: Temporary change in the color of the sclera
options.C: Heavy yellow pus draining from both eyes
options.D: Temporary mild blurriness and slight redness

explanation: Ointments coat the surface of the eye, causing brief blurriness and mild irritation that quickly clears up. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h6)

question: A mother is worried because her baby's eyes look slightly red and watery an hour after getting eye drops. What is the best initial action?

options.A: Reassure her that this is a normal, temporary reaction to the medication
options.B: Administer an emergency dose of antibiotic eye drops
options.C: Wash the baby's eyes immediately with strong antiseptic soap
options.D: Isolate the baby in a dark room away from bright sunlight

explanation: Mild irritation right after application is a common side effect that goes away without needing special treatment. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is it important for midwives to teach parents about signs of eye infection before discharge?

options.A: So they can spot delayed infections like chlamydia and get early treatment
options.B: Because midwives are not allowed to check newborn eyes at clinic visits
options.C: To ensure they buy private eye drops from the chemist
options.D: To train them to administer prescription antibiotics at home

explanation: Some infections appear days after birth when the baby is already at home, making parent awareness vital. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a safe practice for parents caring for a newborn's eyes at home?

options.A: Washing hands thoroughly before touching the baby's face
options.B: Looking out for any unusual yellow discharge
options.C: Wiping both eyes with the same unwashed cloth
options.D: Keeping scheduled postnatal checkup appointments

explanation: Using the same cloth or failing to wash hands can easily spread bacteria from one eye to another. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T4#BMP214_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary substance that covers a newborn's skin at birth?

options.A: Lanugo hair
options.B: Meconium residue
options.C: Vernix caseosa
options.D: Amniotic fluid

explanation: Vernix caseosa is the whitish, cheesy substance found on the skin of a newborn at birth, which provides protection and moisture. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why should healthcare providers avoid scrubbing off all the vernix caseosa right after birth?

options.A: It acts as a natural moisturizer and protector
options.B: It prevents neonatal jaundice
options.C: It helps the cord dry faster
options.D: It is needed for the first stool

explanation: Leaving vernix on the skin helps protect against infections and keeps the newborn's skin hydrated. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h1)

question: How long do current guidelines recommend waiting before giving a newborn their first bath?

options.A: Only 30 minutes
options.B: At least 24 hours
options.C: Exactly 2 hours
options.D: Up to one week

explanation: Delaying the bath for at least 24 hours helps stabilize the baby's temperature and blood sugar. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h2)

question: A mother wants to bathe her baby just one hour after birth. What is the best response?

options.A: Use cold water to wake the baby
options.B: Tell her newborns must never be bathed
options.C: Advise waiting to prevent the baby from getting cold and to help with breastfeeding
options.D: Take the baby for a full soap bath right away

explanation: Early bathing risks hypothermia and interferes with skin-to-skin contact and early feeding. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which part of the newborn's body should be washed first during a bath?

options.A: The back
options.B: The feet
options.C: The face
options.D: The hair

explanation: Washing the face first with plain water prevents soap from getting into the baby's eyes and mouth. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why is it important to dry skin folds carefully after bathing a newborn?

options.A: It is the only way to remove stubborn vernix
options.B: It stimulates the baby's nervous system
options.C: Trapped moisture can lead to skin irritation and rashes
options.D: It prevents birthmarks from forming

explanation: Moisture trapped in warm skin folds creates an ideal breeding ground for germs and causes rashes. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the recommended approach for routine umbilical cord care?

options.A: Daily antiseptic scrubbing
options.B: Covering with tight bandages
options.C: Dry cord care
options.D: Applying palm oil

explanation: Keeping the cord clean and dry allows it to fall off naturally without introducing harmful substances. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which practice should be strictly discouraged when teaching parents about cord care?

options.A: Folding the diaper below the navel
options.B: Allowing the cord stump to be exposed to air
options.C: Washing the abdomen gently with clean water
options.D: Applying traditional herbal mixtures or oils to the stump

explanation: Substances like oils or herbs trap moisture and bacteria, significantly increasing the risk of serious infection. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h4)

question: How often do healthy newborns generally need to be bathed?

options.A: Three times every day
options.B: Only once a month
options.C: Two to three times a week
options.D: Whenever they cry

explanation: Newborns do not get dirty quickly, and bathing them too often dries out their delicate skin. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h5)

question: A mother is worried about tiny white bumps on her newborn's nose. How should the midwife respond?

options.A: Advise her to stop breastfeeding
options.B: Prescribe a strong antibiotic cream
options.C: Tell her to squeeze the bumps firmly
options.D: Reassure her that these are milia and will clear up on their own

explanation: Milia are normal, harmless blocked glands that resolve spontaneously without any intervention. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h5)

question: What type of skin care products should a midwife recommend for daily use on a newborn?

options.A: Alcohol-based cleaning solutions
options.B: Fragrance-free and mild products made for infants
options.C: Strong medicated soaps for adults
options.D: Highly perfumed oils

explanation: Infant skin is sensitive and absorbs chemicals easily, so gentle, fragrance-free products prevent irritation and allergies. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h6)

question: Why are heavily perfumed baby products discouraged by midwives?

options.A: They cause rapid weight loss
options.B: They can cause allergic reactions and skin irritation
options.C: They prevent the umbilical cord from falling off
options.D: They make the hair grow too fast

explanation: Chemical additives and fragrances in perfumed products easily irritate fragile neonatal skin. [learn more](BMP214_U2_T5#BMP214_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for producing breast milk after delivery?

options.A: Estrogen
options.B: Progesterone
options.C: Oxytocin
options.D: Prolactin

explanation: Prolactin is the key hormone produced by the pituitary gland that makes milk after childbirth. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why does full milk production usually wait until after pregnancy?

options.A: The infant has not yet stimulated the neural receptors
options.B: High levels of estrogen and progesterone block milk production
options.C: The alveoli are not yet fully formed until labor starts
options.D: Oxytocin levels are too high to allow synthesis

explanation: During pregnancy, high levels of placenta hormones keep milk production on hold until the placenta is delivered. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h1)

question: During which stage of lactogenesis does the large increase in milk volume known as 'milk coming in' happen?

options.A: Lactogenesis II
options.B: Lactogenesis III
options.C: Galactopoiesis
options.D: Lactogenesis I

explanation: Lactogenesis II happens within the first few days after birth when the milk volume increases significantly. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h2)

question: A mother who gave birth 36 hours ago is worried she is only producing small drops of colostrum. What is the best response?

options.A: Advise immediate formula supplementation due to a failure in Lactogenesis I
options.B: Instruct her to stop feeding until Lactogenesis III initiates automatically
options.C: Reassure her that copious milk flow typically begins between 48 and 72 hours postpartum
options.D: Check her hormone levels for an absence of prolactin receptors

explanation: Full milk volume usually starts by the third day after birth, so small amounts of colostrum early on are completely normal. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the main job of oxytocin during breastfeeding?

options.A: Suppressing estrogen to maintain milk supply
options.B: Stimulating nerve endings in the infant's mouth
options.C: Contracting myoepithelial cells to eject milk
options.D: Synthesizing proteins inside the alveolar cells

explanation: Oxytocin causes the tiny muscles around the milk glands to squeeze, pushing milk forward into the ducts. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h3)

question: How can emotional stress or severe pain affect breastfeeding?

options.A: By inhibiting the release of oxytocin and blocking the milk ejection reflex
options.B: By directly destroying prolactin molecules inside the anterior pituitary gland
options.C: By causing the infant to permanently reject the milk ducts
options.D: By increasing progesterone production to stop Lactogenesis III

explanation: Stress triggers adrenaline, which can block oxytocin and make it harder for milk to flow out. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which sugar is found in the highest amount in human breast milk?

options.A: Lactose
options.B: Glucose
options.C: Fructose
options.D: Sucrose

explanation: Lactose is the primary sugar in human milk, giving the baby energy and helping brain development. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why is having more whey protein than casein helpful for a newborn baby?

options.A: It forms softer curds that are much easier for immature digestive tracts to process
options.B: It speeds up the infant's metabolic rate to prevent neonatal jaundice
options.C: It completely replaces the need for any maternal antibodies
options.D: It prevents the infant from absorbing excess water during hot weather

explanation: Whey proteins digest quickly and easily in a baby's stomach compared to tougher casein curds. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h4)

question: What main immune substance is found in very high amounts in colostrum?

options.A: Folic acid
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Caseinogen
options.D: Secretory IgA

explanation: Colostrum is rich in secretory IgA, which helps protect the newborn's gut and mucous membranes from germs. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why is colostrum often called the newborn's first immunization?

options.A: It provides concentrated antibodies and protective factors that guard the gut against infections
options.B: It stimulates the bone marrow to produce white blood cells immediately
options.C: It contains live attenuated viruses that trigger active antibody production
options.D: It completely replaces the need for routine childhood immunizations later

explanation: Colostrum contains high levels of antibodies that coat the baby's digestive tract to fight off bacteria and viruses. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h5)

question: How does the fat content of hindmilk compare to foremilk at the start of a feeding?

options.A: Hindmilk contains virtually no fat compared to foremilk
options.B: Foremilk has higher fat content to satisfy immediate hunger
options.C: Foremilk and hindmilk have identical lipid concentrations
options.D: Hindmilk has a significantly higher fat and calorie content

explanation: Milk gets fatter as the feeding goes on, making hindmilk much richer in calories than the watery foremilk at the start. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h6)

question: A mother switches her baby between breasts every five minutes to keep times equal, but the baby stays fussy and is not gaining weight well. What is the likely reason?

options.A: The infant is experiencing a total failure of Lactogenesis I
options.B: The baby is receiving mostly low-fat foremilk and missing out on calorie-dense hindmilk
options.C: Frequent switching destroys secretory IgA molecules inside the milk ducts
options.D: The rapid switching prevents prolactin from reaching the anterior pituitary gland

explanation: Short feeds mean the baby only drinks the foremilk and misses the richer hindmilk needed for fullness and weight gain. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T1#BMP214_U3_T1_h6)

question: What part of the breast should ideally be taken into the baby's mouth during a deep latch?

options.A: A large portion of the areola
options.B: The Montgomery glands exclusively
options.C: Only the tip of the nipple
options.D: The upper quadrant of the breast

explanation: Taking a large part of the areola ensures the baby compresses the milk ducts properly rather than pinching just the sensitive nipple tissue. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T2#BMP214_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why does latching onto only the nipple cause severe pain and poor milk transfer for the mother?

options.A: Saliva reacts negatively with the outer skin of the areola
options.B: The milk ducts instantly close when touched by lips
options.C: The nipple gets crushed between the baby's gums and tongue
options.D: The infant's nose blocks the airway during shallow feeding

explanation: A shallow latch leaves the nipple exposed to direct friction and compression from the hard gums, causing trauma and pain. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T2#BMP214_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which breastfeeding position works best for a mother recovering from a recent Caesarean section to protect her abdominal wound?

options.A: Football hold
options.B: Traditional cradle hold
options.C: Standing upright hold
options.D: High cradle position

explanation: The football hold keeps the baby's weight tucked under the mother's arm and away from her healing lower abdomen and incision. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T2#BMP214_U3_T2_h2)

question: Which hand supports the baby's head and neck during a cross-cradle hold?

options.A: The hand closer to the mother's hip
options.B: Both hands joined together under the baby's back
options.C: The hand on the same side as the feeding breast
options.D: The hand opposite to the feeding breast

explanation: Using the opposite hand allows the mother to firmly cup the base of the neck and guide the baby's head precisely to the breast. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T2#BMP214_U3_T2_h2)

question: What parts of the baby's body must form a straight line during proper feeding alignment?

options.A: Head, spine, and ankles
options.B: Nose, chin, and toes
options.C: Eyes, chest, and knees
options.D: Ear, shoulder, and hip

explanation: Keeping the ear, shoulder, and hip aligned prevents the baby's neck from twisting, which makes swallowing difficult. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T2#BMP214_U3_T2_h3)

question: Why should the mother move the baby to the breast rather than leaning her breast down toward the baby?

options.A: The baby will refuse to open its mouth if the breast moves
options.B: Gravity pulls the milk out of the ducts too quickly
options.C: Moving the breast stops the let-down reflex from occurring
options.D: Leaning forward causes poor spinal posture and a shallow, painful latch

explanation: Leaning down strains the mother's back and usually results in an off-center, shallow attachment that damages the nipple. [learn more](BMP214_U3_T2#BMP214_U3_T2_h3)

question: What does a distinct pause in the baby's chin movement indicate during breastfeeding?

options.A: The milk supply has completely run dry
options.B: The baby is actively swallowing milk
options.C: The infant is experiencing a mild cramp
